If I understand correctly, because this is rather complicated, the humanitarian convoy, which was supposed to carry food and aid, this convoy called "Ahmet" [as interpreted] was supplied in Zagreb, that's where it went to fetch the weapons, and then these were put on the trucks. And then there was a police control, and these arms were discovered on board these trucks. According to you, did these weapons come from Zagreb or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you say that these weapons came from Zagreb. According to you, if we look at the numbering of these weapons, and in light of the equipment here, do you believe that this was provided by the Republic of Croatia or was this done without the Republic of Croatia knowing about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Frankly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't know. Because there are two possibilities. Either Ahmet [as interpreted] has weapons delivered, and we don't know where the weapons come from, from which country they come from, and this agency then carries these weapons in the direction of the ABiH, or it is the Republic of Croatia that supports all of this and has the weapons carried under the cover of a humanitarian convoy. But you can't answer my question, can you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all I can infer, based on this, is this: If they could take delivery without any hindrance at all in Croatia, then I suspect that the weapons came from a different source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But did you have a look at these weapons? We have a list and the reference numbers before us. Where did these weapons come from, according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't remember. There were so many weapons passing through my warehouse, it's difficult to remember all the specifics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you can't say anything about it. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I can't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me now turn to the Defence counsel of the other accused. Mr. Kovacic, third Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The Praljak Defence has no any question to this witness. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Petkovic Defence has no questions for this witness, either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fifth Defence team. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 6D.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. We have no questions, although we do wish to thank the gentleman for coming here to give his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, it might be a good idea to have the break now and start off your cross-examination after the break. What do you think? Ms. West, would you like to start straight away?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, everyone on the Chamber, and everyone in and around the courtroom. I could start right now, if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Majic. My name is Kim West. I'm from the Office of the Prosecution, and I'm going to ask you some questions.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The questions I will ask you, many of them, to start off with, will actually include the Defence binder, so if you could have both of those accessible. I'm just going to go back to the testimony from this last hour, in which you indicated, in answer to a question, that the HVO and the BH Army cooperated in certain areas. Would you clarify for us in what areas that the BH Army and the HVO Army cooperated?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't do that. I don't have that kind of knowledge. I can't be specific about it, and I don't want to commit.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But nonetheless, you understood that there was cooperation; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, in several different places.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that cooperation also existed over different periods of time; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, for example, that cooperation between the HVO and the Muslims, the BH Army, would include much of 1992 in Mostar. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that cooperation would even creep into the beginning of 1993 in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, that's correct, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so when Judge Antonetti asked you quite candidly whether you would give weapons to friends or enemies, you indicated that you would give weapons to friends. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember, and it's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so those friends would include the BH Army in Mostar, at least in 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that those friends would also include the BH Army in Mostar in the early part of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Although you've indicated that you have limited knowledge of the cooperation, would you agree with me that there was also cooperation in other areas of Bosnia? An example of that would be the Posavina area?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: My information suggests that that is true. I don't have that much information or close information just to be sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And recently the Trial Chamber heard from Stipo Buljan, who is the head of welfare for the HVO in the Posavina and, later, the Republic. And at page 36822, he was posed this question, and the question was: "And so you'll agree with me that when the Muslims and Croats were fighting each other in Mostar in 1993, the Muslims and Croats were cooperating with each other in Posavina?" And his answer was: "Yes, that's right." Mr. Majic, is that consistent with your understanding as well?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, generally speaking, that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree with me that another area of cooperation was in Sarajevo in 1992 and for part of 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And recently the Trial Chamber heard from Dragan Pinjuh that in Sarajevo, they were cooperating up until November of 1993, and that was in regard to a question before Judge Antonetti, and that is the following, where the question was: "In other words, until November of 1993, the HVO and the ABiH had a common enemy, the Serbs?" And the answer was: "Yes." Sir, do you agree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, we had the same enemy. I can tell you, from my own experience, that we never considered the BH Army to be a real enemy. I said something a while ago to the effect that when the Serbs wanted to make it easier on themselves, they would infiltrate their own agents to stir up trouble between the Croats and the Bosniaks, which then made their lives easier, for at least a year and a half, until the Washington Accords were signed, and then we joined forces again to free our territories from the enemy that we shared, the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, in regard to that issue, today Judge Antonetti asked you whether you considered the Muslims to be brothers-in-arms or friends, and your response to that question was: "I personally did not consider them to be my enemies." And so my question to you is: If you personally did not believe that, did you know other people who did consider them to be your enemies?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. What is the relevance of all of this, and what does it have to do with this gentleman's testimony? It's beyond the scope of direct examination and it's totally irrelevant. There was a conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, what is the relevance of your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, this -- this witness is being brought here to indicate to you that the HVO gave weapons and supplies to the BiH Army equally and without disregard to when the request came in. This gentleman indicated that he had no personal animosity towards the Muslims. Obviously, it's the -- it's the Prosecution's case that there was an animosity, and I'm asking him to speak further on that particular issue. This was a question that was brought up by the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may briefly respond. First of all, this gentleman can't speak for anybody else. He's speaking for himself. Secondly, we've had testimony about the enormous amount of help that the ABiH was receiving from the Republic of Croatia as well as from the Croats within Bosnia-Herzegovina. I fail to see the relevance of this line of questioning, keeping in mind that there is a conflict that goes on for a period of time off and on in different areas, and in different areas there's a different level of cooperation, and also keeping in mind that if she's going to go into that, that perhaps she should also ask the gentleman how much of the arms and funding that Izetbegovic was receiving from the Islamic community, how much of that was going into their warehouses. That is a question that I would really like to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, good afternoon. With respect, I would join my learned friend Mr. Karnavas' objection in this regard. The question is, in fact, extremely wide. Of course, it may well be the case that in a population, there are a number of disparate views. That is hardly a matter of controversy between the parties. Your Honours, the reason this witness is being called is the core evidence, and I'd ask my learned friend to controvert -- seek to controvert that, is that a lot of weapons were given to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, Your Honour, the other issues are somewhat tangental, and although the core allegation may not suit the Prosecution's case, the core thrust of this witness's testimony, I would ask Your Honours that the Prosecution be directed to seek to controvert that core aspect, and that is the purpose for which we called this witness. Your Honours, of course, in a community it is not being said for a moment that there is a homogeneous attitude from all the people of a Herceg-Bosna or all the people of Croatia or all the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As an entity, in any pluralistic society there are disparate views, and that is not controverted by the Defence of Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I agree with Mr. Khan, the Croatian Community was not homogeneous, but all the more reason for the witness to tell us what his view on the situation was and how he perceived the situation. This is what Ms. West is trying to highlight. Of course, he can't speak on behalf of other people. What we are interested in is what he thinks about this. Ms. West, put your question. Make sure your question is a precise question, since you want to know what he thinks of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, in your position at the warehouse, having the opportunity to send out supplies and arms to different people, different groups all across Bosnia-Herzegovina, you must have had an opportunity to be in the position to speak to both people from the BH Army and people from the HVO Army; and as a result of those experiences, what is your personal opinion in regard to whether the BH Army or Muslim soldiers were the enemy or the friend of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: From where I stood at the beginning, they were friends, but then, as I said, they were manipulated by - what should I call them? - the instigators of chaos, who wanted to get the two parties to quarrel so that they might then prevail, and these people were our true enemy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said that earlier on, and then Ms. West moved on to something else, but now you return to that previous topic, and I must say that this is the first time I've been hearing this. I'm therefore keenly interested, and I try to understand what you're saying. If I understand properly, on the one hand we have the Serbs, and on the other, the ABiH and the HVO. But then you added this: You said that the Serbs infiltrated between the individuals -- between the ABiH and the HVO, in order to create problems between the ABiH and the HVO. Is that what you said before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour. That's what I had in mind. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a first. This is the first time I'm hearing this. What enables you to say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My information concerning Jugo officers in Yugoslavia, which had a peculiarity, the peculiarity being the appointments of Serbs to all diplomatic positions, to all intelligence positions, because that's what they did, and all this anger and all the defeats that we inflicted on them, they did everything within their power to take revenge, to infiltrate, and to seek out a third enemy, and that's what they were drawing upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But do you have any evidence in support of what you say or are these just thoughts, individual thoughts of yours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a result of my life in Yugoslavia, up until its break-up.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Majic, you've indicated that there was some cooperation in Mostar in 1992, the beginning of 1993, in Posavina and in Sarajevo, so would you agree with me that in those areas it would not have been unusual for the HVO to send supplies to the Muslims or to allow transport of supplies to the Muslims in those areas of cooperation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: No problem at all, as far as I knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And indeed, by doing so, the HVO was helping to fight a common enemy, and in those places the common enemy would have been the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So what I'd like to do now is go through a number of the exhibits that you reviewed with Ms. Nozica. So if you can actually have both binders available to you, and I'd like to categorise each of these exhibits. I'm going to go directly through -- I believe they should be chronological, and the first is 2D00311. Perhaps that's at the end. Do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, this is a document that you testified -- and it was highlighted that Mr. Stojic received this by fax, and that would be the third page. When we go through these documents, we're going to highlight something different about them, and the difference is going to be to where these supplies were going. So would you agree with me that in this case, the person who was responsible for the materials to pick up is Mr. Seta, Suajb from Sarajevo? If you look at the very first page of the B/C/S, it's the first page of the B/C/S, do you see it says responsible individual for material pickup is Mr. Seta, Suajb from Sarajevo; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Suajb Seta. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And as you've already indicated, you would agree that Sarajevo, in March of 1993, was an area of cooperation between the HVO and the BiH?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so this would not be unusual [Realtime transcript read in error "usual"] for the HVO to be allowing distribution of resources to the BH Army in Sarajevo at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's go to 2D00522, and this might be in the beginning of the Defence binder -- of the Defence binder. It's 2D00522, and it's the other binder. My apologies. 522. All right. This is a document that you talked about on direct, and this is signed by Commander Pasalic. And you -- you would agree with me that Arif Pasalic was the commander of the 4th Corps of the BH Army; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this document is dated July 13th, 1992, and would it be fair to say that that is a period of time -- that would be the height of cooperation between the HVO and the BH Army in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: I don't really know about the date when.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Nonetheless, this is 1992, in Mostar, and that was a period of time when the Serbs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Khan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you. Just one correction to the transcript. Page 57, line 5, I believe my learned friend's question, accurately put, was that it would not be unusual, rather than usual, which the transcript currently reads. I believe that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. That is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, sir, July of 1992, this is a period of time within a month after the HVO and the BiH got the Serbs out of Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So if you can go to 2D00523, it should be just the next one.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This is another request from Commander Pasalic. It's October 1992, and the very first sentence says: "Considering upcoming combat actions and the tasks of the 1st Mostar Brigade, we require the following type of ... ammunition ..." Would you also agree with me that this is another document that was issued in 1992 when the HVO and the BH Army were cooperating together in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: I agree. As far as the dates are concerned, if that's what's indicated, well, then, no reason not to believe it. Right?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And there was also no reason to not help the Muslim Army with ammunition and hand-grenades during that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, what you're saying is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If you can go to the next document. It should just be the next one, 524. This is a document that you looked at earlier. It's dated December 1992. It's from a commander, and it says: "Considering the combat actions by our brigade in the area of Igman on breaking the blockade around the city of Sarajevo, we are contacting you with a request ..." So this regards sending MTS to Sarajevo. This was a period of time when the BH Army and the HVO were cooperating in Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: I really can't say what happened when. I don't know the dates, because I just worked in the warehouse. Let me repeat that. I took delivery of goods and issued them out, and I didn't see most of the items, and I don't know what happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina when -- when the conflict broke out and so on, and I keep saying this. As far as I'm concerned, there were no conflicts between us and the BH Army, and not from my superiors, either, those of them who are in court here today.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I know you say that as far as you're concerned and for some of the superiors who are in the courtroom today that there was no conflict, you would agree that starting in a -- sometime in 1993, that there was conflict in Herceg-Bosna between the HVO and the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Indubitably, yes, you can't avoid that. I can't say that there wasn't a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you've not shown us today a document in the binder in front of you that shows any distribution of MTS to the BH Army after even February of 1993, have you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to object. This is a very imprecise question, because we did see documents dating till after February, but the Prosecutor has to say to whom and when, and does it mean that if they were not contained in the binder that they don't exist? Yes, we have seen documents after February 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, you may be wrong. We have a document dated 6th of March, 2D1041.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Let's go straight to that. That's 2D01041.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this is a document dated March 6th, correct, 1993, and it says: "By which it is approved for which Mr. Ismet Mehmedovic from Gradac [sic], uninterrupted transport on the route from Ploce to Gradac [sic], of the following equipment." So you would agree with me that Ploce is -- that's a Croatian port; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it says "passing through," en route to, Ploce-Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And Gradac [sic] is in the Posavina, is it not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: In part, yes, but who is taking delivery of the MTS here we see is Mr. Ismet -- I can't -- it's not quite legible.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And, sir, my question to you is: Gradac [sic], and I think I'm -- I'm sure I'm pronouncing that incorrectly, that's in the area of the Posavina, is it not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in March of 1993, there was cooperation between the HVO and the BH Army in the Posavina, was there not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Well, I do have reason not to believe. I don't have that information, to be quite frank.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Prosecution is suggesting something that quite simply is not correct. Now, if the witness doesn't know, he can say he doesn't know, but Gradacac at this point in time is part of Tuzla, and it goes to the Tuzla Corps, that delivery. And so the Prosecutor wishes to introduce a maximum of confusion into this -- these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently Gradacac is close to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Assuming we take that as testimony from Mr. Praljak, then even if Gradac [sic] isn't part of Tuzla, Tuzla was also a place of cooperation between the HVO and the BH Army, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't agree with taking anything as testimony from Mr. Praljak. He'll have the opportunity to give testimony at the proper time. But on occasion, it is of assistance to the parties to have clarification. And of course the Prosecution, being desirous of getting to the truth, if a fact has been clarified, it only behooves them to put it based -- squarely to the witness as to whether or not that clarification will help Your Honours get to the truth. So, Your Honours, I would ask that a very straightforward question be put to the witness, not on the basis of any evidence given by Mr. Praljak, but on the basis of a clarification that hopefully will assist the Prosecution to perform their functions, which is to very squarely and fairly put the evidence before Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, let's continue on with the Posavina, because I'd like to get to these documents. We'll go back to where we ended, which is 2D00630. You may have to go back a little bit. 630.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have an answer, with the greatest of respect, to the question. So perhaps either the question can be withdrawn or the question can be properly and squarely put, as I've requested. But there is no answer to the question put by my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you may know this or you may not. Is Gradacac in Posavina or is it close to Tuzla, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Near Tuzla. Now, geography -- well, judging by who is taking delivery of the goods, then it's quite obvious that it's for the BH Army units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, Tuzla was an area of cooperation between the HVO and the BiH Army as well, was it not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can we put P10887 on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This might be helpful to us, sir. This is a map of the front-lines in July of 1993, but more simply, it's just a map of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So we see, if you look in the upper sort of right corner, you see Gradac [sic]. Do you see that? There is a red line, a red Serb front-line running right through it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And assuming that red Serb front-line is accurate, you would agree with me that in that area, there was a Serb front, a Serb front-line?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of this, but I am really not a reader of maps. I don't have the knowledge, personally, how to read this map correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Would you also agree that that area, that general area up there, is, if not the Posavina, very close to the Posavina and just north of Tuzla, both areas of cooperation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, based on this map, Gradacac is quite a fair bit far away from Tuzla, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some 50 to 70 kilometres removed, on a straight line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know for sure what the distance is.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, while we have the map in front of us, you see the municipality above Gradac [sic], which, I'll spell it, is O-r-a-s-j-e. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you agree with me that that is the area of the Posavina?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Orasje is in Posavina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If we can go to 2D00630.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You looked at this document during direct testimony, and it's October 10th, 1992. It's for issuance of material resources for the needs of Central Rear Base Grude and at the disposal -- or for the HVO 106 Brigade Orasje BiH armed forces. And we had some discussion earlier about whether the BH and HVO had actual forces there, and you remember testifying that you knew at least that there were Bosniaks in the HVO. Do you remember that? I think you have -- I think you'll have to speak louder.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in addition, you would agree with me that these -- and these material resources were going to the area of the Posavina, an area of cooperation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: It would appear to follow from this, but I didn't give it much thought.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you still have the map in front of you? Is the map still on your screen?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can -- is it now?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's there now.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you see, to the west of the town of -- or the municipality of Doboj, west of Gradac [sic], do you see that town?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: What's the name of the town? Yes, I can see Doboj, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now go to 2D00898. This is another document that you looked on -- looked at during direct, and it's an authorisation for transport of materials. And while we're speaking about transport, this is not -- a number of the items -- a number of the documents that you have seen regard two separate things, and I just want to know, to clarify this, one is for the -- the agreement that items can be transported through a particular territory; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And those transport authorisations for ABiH and materials mean that it's the Bosnian-Herzegovina Army's materials, it's just that the HVO is saying, Okay, you can go through this area?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: In certain situations. It went to the Central Logistics Base, directly to me. Then I would be given instructions, and I would issue the goods according to those -- those instructions in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So in this particular case, these items are going ultimately to Doboj; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that's also an area that's close to the Posavina; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you go to the next document, which is just nine --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: I do not have a mike -- [Interpretation] I think I have a right to say something, because I'm from Doboj myself. Doboj is not in Posavina. That's for sure, no. [In English] Not in Posavina.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I had also a comment, a kind of objection. Your Honour, this is the second time the Prosecutor is using the description "it is close to." Well, first, it's very subjective. What is close to maybe your friend is not close to me. I can walk, she cannot walk, et cetera, et cetera. Particularly -- particularly in the conditions of war, something was very close, but, for example, in some cases there is a huge mountain in between, this is another country, this is like it is in Australia. So I think we should be very precise. Is it part of the region, meaning communication of people, goods, et cetera, or it is entirely another word. It cannot be "close." There is no close position in the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, can you go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, I'm sure you have understood what the problem is. You are saying "close to." What does this mean, exactly?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do understand what the problem is, but I would submit that the theme of my cross-examination is of no surprise to anyone. What we are doing is going through each of these documents to show that when the HVO was giving supplies or authorising transport of these materials to the BH Army, they were not doing it as a favour to the BH Army, they were doing it because it was in their own interests. These are all areas of cooperation. Had any of these counsel asked to -- asked questions on cross-examination, they could have explored this very issue. But with all due respect to my learned friend who's from Doboj, that is not an appropriate comment to make as an objection. I did say "close to Posavina." I was careful about that, but to be clear, it seems unusual to me to hear these types of -- these types of objections during my cross-examination when none of them took an opportunity to do the cross themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I make it clear that it has not been asserted, on behalf of Mr. Stojic, that the provision of weapons was a favour to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. No doubt there are mutual interests. Even in friendships -- the question of friendships was raised by Your Honours. Even in friendships, they have to be reciprocal, if they are to be lasting. So, Your Honours, as far as that's concerned, the response of my learned friend really doesn't have legs, in my respectful submission. Your Honour, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Khan, it seems to me you're pleading, you're presenting arguments to the merits, and I wonder whether this is really the moment to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is, in my respectful submission, because if one reads what -- Your Honour, perhaps Your Honour could be patient before just moving on. I would invite Your Honour to read exactly what my learned friend Ms. West very eloquently put about the theme of her cross-examination, and she went into that. That is not a response to an objection. The objection put forward by me is not the lack of notice by my learned friend. I'm not surprised in the least regarding the area she's seeking to go into, but it's a question of precision. That was the form of objection that my learned friends raised, a question of precision, not notice regarding theme. And to that extent, Your Honours, it is my respectful submission that my objection and those of my colleagues for the other teams should be sustained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall now have a 20-minute break, since it is now time to have a break. We shall resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, you have 46 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Majic, I'm going to ask you to go to the bigger binder now. And if you can please go to 2D01250, and it's in the back. It's 2D01250. It's a yellow tab. This is a February 14th, 1993, letter from Commander Pasalic again of the Muslim Army, and in it he is asking the HVO to take possession and transport a number of items for the 4th Corps. And it gives the list of the resources, and it indicates materials and equipment for the needs of the ABiH 4th Corps forces, and because of the possible offensive by the Chetniks, it is necessary that "you immediately issue a permit for uninterrupted passage of the transport via ..." and then it goes through these towns, and it goes through Visoko, which you mentioned earlier was the ABiH Logistics Centre; right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But if you go to the second page of the English, but I -- it's your first page in the B/C/S, it says: "We have contacted you with this request earlier on January 15th, 1993, but you have not permitted the transport." Mr. Majic, February of 1993, you -- this was when you were working at the warehouse; correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you were also there the month earlier, January 15th, 1993; right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: January? Yes, January, the first month, "sijecanj," January.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You worked at the warehouse in January as well; yes?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: I don't understand. Yes, in January, yes. We call the month "Sijecanj," January.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you remember a request like this coming through on January 15th from Commander Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: No. I apologise, but I didn't receive requests like this. My superiors received the requests, and then when they issued instructions for distribution, then I would act upon those instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's correct. You testified that it was the distribution you would receive; right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right, order for distribution.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And on January 15th, do you ever remember receiving an order for distribution for this request?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I would say rather yes than no, but I can't claim for sure, because how do I know order for distribution? I would be more than a computer if I could remember all the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Fair enough --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for getting to my feet, but I'd like to ask my learned friend that in the introduction -- say that in the introduction, it is an issue of approval, it's an approval for safe passage. It is not an order for distribution. It is an approval for safe passage for the goods. So when she asks the witness whether he received an order for distribution, she cannot base her question on this document, because this is approval for transport, not approval for distribution of the MTS.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll accept that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, but again if we focus on page 2 of the English, where it says: "We have contacted you with this request earlier on January 15th, 1993, but you have not permitted the transport," my question to you is, are you aware on that date of an ultimatum being issued by Mr. Prlic indicating that all units of the BH Army should be subordinated to the HVO and giving a dead-line of five days?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: No, I don't have that knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And may I object for the record, Your Honour. According to the question, it is that Prlic issued. I think we've gone around and round on this, and I think it's an imprecise -- and I know the Prosecution, like a broken record, wishes and wishes to mention it and hopefully it will become history, but that is not the case. This was a decision taken by a collective body, and let's address it as that. Whether it was an ultimatum or not, I leave it for the Court. So I would also object to that characterisation of that particular decision. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll move on. He indicated he doesn't have any knowledge, anyways.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, if you can go to P01499 in the binder in front of you, 1499. So this is a document that's dated February 16th, 1993. This is just two days later than the other document I just showed you, and it's a request again from -- no, excuse me, it looks like it's from the chief of the Defence Department, Mr. Mijo Anjic [phoen], but it's a list of technical and motor equipment for the 108th HVO Brcko Brigade. But what I'd like to focus on, on the B/C/S on the side, you see a handwritten note, and that note says: "Dear Mr. Jarnjak, please inform Ploce, Mr. Redzo, to let these means pass to HVO Grude and up." I'll just stop for a moment. Mr. Majic, it's on the side of the B/C/S. You see it's written up the side, it's handwritten. So it's -- yeah, there you go. So it's the handwritten language up the side, and I'm going to read that. It says: "Please inform Ploce to let these means pass to HVO Grude. Please intensify the control of loading of humanitarian aid in Split. Muslims are smuggling weapons using these -- those convoys. Sincerely yours," and then it says, "Slobodan," and the English says "family name illegible," but if you look at the B/C/S, I would submit that says "Slobodan Praljak." Do you see that handwriting?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do see that, but as far as I'm concerned, it doesn't mean anything. It's not indicative of anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, if I were to suggest to you that it might be indicative of Mr. -- or the signatory was concerned about Muslims having weapons, Muslims are smuggling weapons using these convoys, would you agree with that, that there's some concern there?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Calls for speculation. Objection. The text stands for what it says right there. As to what interpretation or spin should be given to the text, that would be left to the Judges, not for this witness to speculate. That's not proper evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, don't forget that the witness has -- since he was working in the Logistics Centre and was taking delivery of material and equipment, he only has a piecemeal understanding of all of this. Anything more complicated goes beyond the scope of his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Majic, you have testified that there were places and times where the HVO and the Croats cooperated together. Were there also places and times when the HVO and the Serbs cooperated together?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: No, I don't have that knowledge myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. But would you agree with me that the Grude Logistics Base was also the source of supplies to -- sometimes to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: I don't have that knowledge. In my sector, where I was in charge of the MTS, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at P08118. It's P08118. This is the annual report for the Supplies Procurement/Production Sector for 1993, and this the group with whom you worked; right? This is where you worked?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I was not involved in producing this, this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I understand that. And if you go to the second page of the English, there's a sort of a cover page, and it's signed by Ante Jelavic. He was your supervisor; right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, I understand that you did not take part in writing this, but I'd like to go over a couple of the comments in here to see if you can shed any light on them. If you can go to page 20 of the English, but the B/C/S is date-stamped "0346-9369."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And I think, Mr. Usher, he will probably need some help with this. It ends in "369."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Maybe I'll just read this out in English, but the B/C/S ends in -- it's date-stamped 0346-9369, it ends in 369, and it's the last sentence on the page. But in English this is talking about fuel, and it's under the heading of "Realisation of set tasks." And in the English, it says: "The transport of fuel for 'X' by fuel truck convoys was directly organised by the transport administration and effected by the transport company." Mr. Majic, do you have any idea what that sentence means and who -- what is the identity of X?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: No, no idea. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm just going to show you -- it's page 25 of the English, and the B/C/S ends in "416." Can you hear?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: It's back.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this is under the heading of "Procurement of TTS," and in English it's the bottom of the page -- or for the B/C/S, it's the second paragraph, and it says: "Fuel for side X was obtained by the Technical and Procurement Administrations. This obstructed in planning of consumption and caused additional problems in terms of procurement, transport, and meeting expenses." Mr. Majic, does that second reading of this report give you an understanding of what "X" means?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know, I really don't. I was a deputy, but I was attached to the Construction Administration. Frankly, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Majic, have you ever heard of the XY side?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Frankly, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm going to read some testimony to you and see if we can explore this further.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object, Your Honour, to this line of questioning. The gentleman has already indicated that he doesn't know what X is, or XY, or XYZ, or whatever the case may be, so reading testimony to somehow get the witness to vouch for something is improper. At this point, this is beyond the scope of the gentleman's knowledge, and I think we need to appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, Mr. Karnavas has just said something important. It is beyond the scope of the gentleman's knowledge. You are trying to introduce, through him, data that we have available, because this has been addressed already. But obviously the witness is not aware of this, so it's a waste of time. What's the point of it? He does not know that there might have been some kind of "cooperation," quote/unquote, with the Serbs, as might be indicated by the document. He said that three times in a row, he said, "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. However, what this witness should be able to testify in regard to is whether any supplies went out of Grude for XY, and those are the documents I'm about to get into.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If the gentleman doesn't know what XY is, Your Honour, I don't see how it helps. It really -- at this point in time, Your Honour, you do need to issue an instruction for our learned friend to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we're going to go straight -- cut to the chase, because this could go forever. From where you were, from Grude, from the Logistics Base, as far as you know, was there to be addressed to the Serbs weapons, ammunition, fuel, that was sent, as seems to be indicated by this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, certainly not. I have no knowledge of that at all. That is where we should begin. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Ms. West, he's been saying this four times, saying that he doesn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to move on to P04272. We're going to move off of X, but I'd like to continue to talk about any knowledge you might have about HVO and Serb cooperation. This is an ECMM report, and I would just note that the document, I think, cannot be shown publicly on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, again I'm going to have a standing objection. We need to move on on this. Trying to force the gentleman into saying something that he doesn't know or to get him to speculate is not helpful to anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Prosecutor, you are stubborn. The witness was adamant, he said he didn't know, and now you come up with a document from an international organisation, so obviously he doesn't know a thing, not the first thing about it, in order to return to the topic. What a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, most respectfully, I disagree. The issue with this witness is whether Grude was supplying Muslims in areas of cooperation, to which he has provided this Court with an answer that they have. What I would like to show is that Grude was also supplying weapons and arms and supplies to the Serbs. Since he was based at Grude, and he may not know what "XY" means, but since he's based at Grude and he's getting a distribution order from Ante Jelavic, he should be able to comment on what sort of items are going out of Grude.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I most respectfully submit that if that is their theory, that perhaps they could put it or they should have put it through their witnesses, but to now try to get the gentleman to somehow agree that they were supplying the Serbs as they were supplying the Muslims, this is not the time or place or individual. You know, I would love to debate this point, and I will continue to debate this point, but we need to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, if you want to waste your time, go ahead, but you know, Madam Prosecutor, I read the Milutinovic judgement. In the Milutinovic case, the Prosecution had asked for 260 hours. It used only 160 hours. So I suppose that your colleagues from the Milutinovic case made best use of their time. Now you are wasting it. Go ahead, if you so wish.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Majic, you indicated that up until at least May of 1993, you were in charge of the warehouse which is located in the forest; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, up until mid-May 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in mid-May of 1993, where did your office -- where did you move to?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: I was deputy assistant head, and the head was Mr. Jelavic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so my question is: Physically, where was your office located?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: My office was at Zenicka Street. I had a room that I was using there, an office. But as I said before, when I moved and started working as Jelavic's deputy, I was mostly involved in construction, rebuilding, and everything else that we needed. Later, we started rebuilding roads. So after this date, that was what my involvement was about and continued to be about, just that, until the day I retired.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in your office on that street, is that -- is that the same building where Mr. Jelavic had his office as well?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, the same building.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And was he on your same floor?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, same floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And was Mr. Boban's office on the same floor?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: No. Mr. Boban's office was in the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that's a different building?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, a different building altogether.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When you moved to that location in May of 1993, how long were you in that location? Did I understand that it was until you retired?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, until I retired.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I? Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Majic, it might be helpful if you would tell us, so that we also have it in the record, in which town is Zenicka Street?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Zenicka is what we call the building, not the street, the former premises of the RNK Zenicka, but this was in Grude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said something that I found interesting, because so far I was wondering where Mr. Boban's office was, and you are telling us about it. You've just said that Mr. Boban's office was in the Town Hall of Grude; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know -- well, did you know the City Hall, did you go to that building?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am from Grude. I was in the Municipal Council, so yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there is a room, a council room, in the Municipal Council building. I suppose that there was an office for the president of the council, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And was Mr. Boban in that office that would be, by tradition, reserved for the president of the Grude Municipal Council?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: The municipal president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he was -- occupied the office of the president of the municipality. See, you came to speak about logistics, but I am interested in offices, in premises. Sometimes it boils down to one and the same thing. Did he have a lot of offices next to his, Mr. Boban's, or was it very small? Like the people working for him, did they have offices or was it just a very small structure?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we went on location, we should have gone to visit the Municipal Council building. We would have seen the premises. We didn't think of it then, but if we go there again, we'll go there. Ms. Nozica, do you have any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, two additional clarifications in relation to two documents, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Majic, you have my binder, you have the OTP binder. Can you please go back to the following document. It's a document in my binder, 2D311. You've got it. Thank you. We have a date here, the 30th of March, 1993, and what we see there is the fact that MTS was issued for the purposes of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, through the Grude Logistics Base. The OTP examined you about this document, but I wish to state this for the record and for the transcript: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Indeed, I do have reason to doubt. This one is addressed to me directly, and then I forwarded it, having received an order to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I don't think you understand me. Do you have any doubt that the MTS was delivered as described by the witness?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, there is no doubt. This is perfectly fair.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we go to another document, please, and I must emphasise that this has been exhibited already. This is 3D0008. You don't have it there, but it's about to appear on the screen in front of you, 3D0008. Just a minute, please. This is an exhibit already, but let us, please, try to look at a number of things here. He received the weapons, and what are the whereabouts of the person who received the weapons on behalf of the BH Army. The date of this document is the 6th of March, 1993. The document specifies certain quantities. Can you please have a closer look and try and explain to the Chamber. We're looking at some equipment for the armed forces. This goes through the Grude Logistics Base. The quantity is 1.000 grenades, one 52 millimetres. This is on the 6th of March, 1993. I'm focusing on grenades, and I'm not taking the bullets into account, the rounds. In your experience, would this not be an enormous amount of weapons and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is simply enormous.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Can we please move on to page 3 of this document in the B/C/S. In the English, it's 3D00002 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, earlier on, I was listening to Ms. West when she was asking you questions, because all the weapons were only used for the Posavina area or Sarajevo, she thought. In this document we have in front of us, Witness, we see people -- three people who are in charge; Seta from Sarajevo, Beslagic from Visoko, and Music from Gradacac. This Beslagic from Visoko, do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did the BiH Army have units in Visoko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I assume so. They had a central logistics base in Visoko as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And to your knowledge - of course we can check that later - did the HVO have a front against the ABiH in or around Visoko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. You don't know. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Sir, could you please look at 3D000025. You will see this is page 3 in e-court, ERN 0183-1697. It's on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] could we please pull the document down slightly -- or pull it up, rather, the other way around. Thank you. There you go.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: There is a note there: "Arrived on the 9th of March in Pazaric and delivered to Dzevad Tirko [phoen]." That's what it says. In connection with the questions asked by my learned friend about whether and where the BH Army was cooperating, and she placed this cooperation in Posavina and in Tuzla, can we please look at the same map that you were shown by my learned friend, P10887, just to make sure about Pazaric and Visoko and their respective locations, that we can have a look. We see that this arrived in Pazaric on the 3rd of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. It may be an error on my part. Could my learned friend please help me with the number of that map that she was showing the witness? I do have the correct number, P10887. It's not correct, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Can we please have a look and can we find Sarajevo on this map, please? Tell me as soon as you've got it. There it is. Look at the map, please, and try to find Visoko. It's above Kiseljak, isn't it? You see that, Witness, don't you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: All right, I see it now. It took some time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Do you see "Visoko," sir, "Breza-Visoko"? Look at number 5, Sarajevo, please. Number 5, marked "Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You do, fine. Okay. Try and have a look, where is the Visoko Logistics Base? Is it in the immediate vicinity of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Majic, is it correct not indisputable that this is nowhere near Posavina or, indeed, Tuzla? This is, in fact, very close to Sarajevo, where the Logistics Base that you were talking about was?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Majic, can you confirm, if we look again at the whole map, that Visoko is in Central Bosnia, in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you speak up, please? I didn't hear you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR MAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Nozica. Yes, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I believe at line 7 through 12 on page 80, the witness that counsel spoke of testified in private session, so I'm wondering if there might be an order of redaction for that part of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall ask the legal officer to check this with the Registrar. Witness, on behalf of my colleagues, I would like to thank you for having to come at the request of Mr. Stojic's Defence counsel to help get to the truth. I wish you a safe journey home, and I shall ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom. Mr. Karnavas, just one moment. Let him leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, will your witness be coming tomorrow or the day after tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, both of our scheduled witnesses, the ones scheduled for Wednesday and Thursday, are yet to arrive. My plan was to have them appear on Wednesday and follow your instructions, one after the other over the course of the same day, if possible. I will be meeting the witnesses tomorrow morning, and we'll be informing the Court of the overall time that I will take to examine these two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand correctly, Ms. Nozica, we will not be able to sit tomorrow afternoon. Ms. Nozica, so there will be no hearing tomorrow afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. You're quite right. I do apologise. My learned friend was making a suggestion, and that was the reason I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, before you take the floor, this is what the Trial Chamber would like to state. I don't know what you're about to say. We handed down a decision at the beginning of this hearing. This ruling is what it is. You can challenge it through the ordinary means, i.e., to certify the decision and to appeal it, but the Trial Chamber holds that once a decision has been handed down, the lawyers are not to challenge it by taking the floor again and say, You have ruled on this and that and I don't agree. If you disagree, then you can appeal the decision. I don't know if that's what you were about to say --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but I anticipated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was not what I was about to say, Your Honour. I do realise that once a decision is made, it is made. I believe there were comments in the past by one of the Judges that we should not try to re-litigate a decision simply because we don't like it, in open court. I did, however, wish to point out one factor, and that is: Because we believe, at least from the tenor of the message, and the tone in which it was delivered, that somehow members of the Trial Chamber are accusing the Prlic Defence team of being underhanded and nefarious in somehow trying to use slight-of-hand techniques in their applications, such as the one that we have, where we went over the word limit. I can assure Your Honours, first and foremost, that since 2001, when I began practicing here, this is the technique that has been used. I've used it in the previous case. Many other Chambers use it. So this is not something that I have come up with. And what I'm speaking of, in particular, is the fact that one can file both a leave and the motion in one particular pleading. It is done very often. It is done routinely, in fact. So there was nothing out of the ordinary. And it seemed, at least from the tenor, that I was somewhat over-recidivist in doing things the wrong way, and of course I just wanted to clarify the record that we chose this method because it was of an urgency and we wanted to get it in. So that was the reason, and I do wish the Trial Chamber to take note of that. We will be filing for a leave to file this again in the way it is, because we do believe that since this is an issue of first impression, which is something that I did not mention, this particular issue, we thought it was necessary to do an extensive briefing to assist you. But be that as it may, I just wanted to clarify the record, Your Honour, that there was no ill intent on the part of the Defence of Dr. Prlic to sneak one on the Court, especially when we, on the very first line or two lines, we state that we are way over the limit. So we hope that you will accept this explanation, because we have been hurt by those comments that somehow we are not being professional, because that was the understanding that we took in the manner in which you delivered your oral decision. And I apologise for having taken -- taking up the time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's on the transcript. We shall, therefore, wait for your submissions. To sum up, we shall meet again on Wednesday. We shall be sitting on Wednesday afternoon. Ms. Nozica will let us know and tell us how much time she will need. As far as we are concerned, we had allocated one hour for each witness. Ms. West, I saw you on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just briefly, just to clarify for the record, the Prosecution will not be responding, then, to the provisional release motion that's been filed, and we will wait to see how this plays out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I wish -- first of all, I'd like to move into private session for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In open session, I would like to state that we shall meet again on Wednesday at a quarter past 2.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 11th day of March, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.46 p.m.,
